01.r: The missionaries the accusers have just named.
01.n: The relative pronoun links this verse to the charge begun in the verse before, which the brief does not show.

02.r: Jason has taken them into his house as guests.
02.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to receive under one's roof, receive as a guest, entertain hospitably', and lists this verse. A perfect: the guests are still with him, which is the point of the charge against Jason.

03.r: The man who gave the missionaries lodging.
03.n: Abbott-Smith lists him in this passage and notes that a Jason named in Paul's letter to the Romans is perhaps the same man.

05.r: The missionaries and those with them.

06.r: Every one of them, without exception.

07.r: Their conduct is set in opposition to Caesar's decrees.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives three senses: 'over against', 'before, in the presence of', and 'against'. He records the last only in this verse.

09.n: From δοκέω, to think or seem; Abbott-Smith gives 'an opinion', then 'a public decree, ordinance', and lists under 'of Roman rulers' this verse and Luke 2:1, on this page. The English 'dogma' comes from it.

10.r: The decrees issued by the emperor.

11.r: Their whole way of acting, as the accusers describe it.
11.n: Abbott-Smith compares this verb to Latin agere, as ποιέω answers to facere, and gives 'to do, practise, be engaged in'. A present tense: an ongoing practice.

12.r: A ruler with a claim to authority alongside Caesar's.
12.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the word was used of the Roman Emperor, as often in common Greek. In this charge, calling Jesus king is presented as acting against Caesar.

13.n: Abbott-Smith notes that this word properly denotes the second of a pair, though in late Greek it overlaps with ἄλλος, other.

14.r: What the accusers say the missionaries teach.

15.r: States the claim reported by the accusers.
15.n: An infinitive, literally 'saying Jesus to be another king', reported speech. The older translations turn it into 'there is another king, one Jesus'; the Greek makes Jesus the subject of the claim.

16.r: The one the missionaries proclaim as king.
16.n: The 'one' in the KJV, Geneva and ASV, and the BSB's 'named', are added in English; the Greek has the name alone.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus has ἕτερον, 'another', in a different position in the last clause, and, as Abbott-Smith notes, spells the verb 'act' πράττουσι. Neither changes the sense, and neither shows in the KJV.
